prime.problem: Checking every substring for contains all of t is O(m²) windows, O(m³) if you recount each one. Comparing two full counters at every step still costs the alphabet size per step.
prime.fits: The first card in Lists, stacks and queues. It builds on the hashing card's O(1) dict updates: a Counter of debts plus one integer turns validity into an O(1) test, so two pointers can sweep once.
expect: need[c]: chars still owed, negative for spares
missing: the sum of positive debts
grow right, shrink left while valid
monotone validity as the condition for shrinking
the k-offset trick for word-sized chunks
prime.goal: Solve Minimum Window Substring in O(|s| + |t|), explain why the left pointer never moves back, and say which window problems break the method.

attend: Why does a single integer missing replace comparing two whole counters?
When the window reads a second B, why doesn't missing change?
Why is it safe to move left forward and never back?
Which property of the question (monotone validity) makes shrinking correct, and which problem on the card lacks it?
For the concatenation problem, why are there exactly k separate windows?

must: need[c] counts what the window still owes (negative = spare) → missing sums only the positive debts → adding a char lowers missing only if it paid a debt → validity is missing == 0, an O(1) test

Validity is monotone (a valid window stays valid when grown, an invalid one stays invalid when shrunk) → once valid, shrink from the left until it breaks → neither pointer ever moves back → each index enters once and leaves once → O(|s| + |t|)
Sum = k with negative numbers is not monotone (dropping a negative raises the sum) → shrinking can skip answers → use a prefix-sum dictionary instead
Word chunks of length k can start at any index → split starts into k offsets, each stepping k letters → each offset is an ordinary counts window over chunks → O(m · k) instead of O(m · n · k)
elevated: Record the answer inside the shrink loop, before dropping s[left] → every minimal valid window is seen once → a tie (CODEBA vs ADOBEC) keeps the earlier best because the test is strict <
reference: the source's C++ packing grow and shrink into one for header
the exact trace rows and the 23 pointer moves
Counter(t) <= window as the slow validity test
at-most(k) − at-most(k − 1) for exactly k distinct

compress.prompt: From memory, write the grow and shrink rules as two lines of pseudocode, then explain in 3 sentences why the whole thing is linear and what property of the problem it depends on.
checklist: grow: if need[ch] > 0 then missing −= 1; need[ch] −= 1
shrink while missing == 0: record, need[s[left]] += 1, if it becomes positive missing += 1, left += 1
each pointer only moves forward, so at most 2|s| moves
validity must be monotone in window size
missing makes validity O(1), not O(alphabet)

retrieve.q: Explain what a negative value in need[c] means and why the algorithm never has to treat it specially.
answer: negative = the window holds spare copies of c beyond what t needs (or c isn't in t at all)
missing only counts positive debts, so spares never change it on the way in
dropping a spare raises need back toward 0 without making missing positive, so the window stays valid

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens at r = 13 when C is added to the window [6, 12): which windows are recorded, and why does the shrink stop at left = 10?
answer: adding C pays the last debt: missing 1 → 0
shrink records ODEBANC (7), DEBANC (6), EBANC (5), BANC (4) while dropping O, D, E
dropping the only B makes need[B] = 1, missing = 1, so the loop stops with left = 10

retrieve.q: You're asked for the longest subarray with sum exactly k, and the array has negatives. Why does this card's method fail, and what do you use instead?
answer: validity isn't monotone: dropping a negative raises the sum, so shrinking can pass over valid windows
the two pointers can no longer each move only forward safely
use a prefix-sum dictionary: store the first index of each prefix sum and look up prefix − k

compare.q: A variable-size counts window vs a fixed-size window with a monotonic deque: what decides when the left end moves in each, and what does each keep about the window's contents?
answer: counts window: left moves while the window is still valid (a condition on counts)
monotonic deque: left moves exactly one step per step, because k is fixed
counts keep a multiset summary (need, missing) and forget order
the deque keeps only the indices that could still be the max, in order

compare.q: Both are two-pointer sweeps where pointers never move back. What invariant justifies never moving back in each, and what breaks it?
answer: here: monotone validity of the window
in sorted-array two pointers: sortedness means moving one pointer can only move the sum one way
both are O(n) because each pointer moves at most n times
negative numbers (here) or unsorted input (there) break the invariant

predict.q: Keep s = "ADOBECODEBANC" but change t to "ABB". Before running: what's the shortest window, and how does needing two Bs change when the window first becomes valid?
predict.answer: BECODEBA (length 8). With need[B] = 2 the window first becomes valid only when the second B arrives: ADOBECODEB, length 10, and it can't shrink because dropping the A breaks it. When the next A arrives at index 10, the left end moves past A, D and O to the first B, giving BECODEBA = s[3:11].

apply.task: Run the card's min_window on s = "ADOBECODEBANC" with t = "ABB" and with t = "AABC", printing need and missing after each r. Then break it: change if need[s[left]] > 0 to >= 0 and describe what goes wrong.
apply.done: You get BECODEBA for ABB and ADOBECODEBA for AABC (both As are needed, so the window can't drop the first A), and you can explain that the broken test counts a spare as a debt, so missing turns positive too early and the loop stops shrinking before the window is minimal.
apply.hint: For AABC the only two As are at indices 0 and 10, so any valid window spans both.
